en.art_refontefr_title: Website Redesign: The Complete Method Without Losing Your SEO (2026)
en.art_refontefr_body:
A website redesign means partially or fully rebuilding an existing site: design, structure, content, technology. Done well, it increases traffic and conversions. Done poorly, it can lose 30 to 70% of organic traffic within weeks — traffic that takes months to come back.

This guide details the method we apply at MSD Media: the 7 steps of a redesign, the full SEO migration checklist, real budgets by provider type, and the most costly mistakes.

When should you redesign your website?

A redesign is justified when your existing site is actively holding your business back. The most reliable signals:

  • The site no longer generates inquiries even though your business is healthy (fewer than 1 contact per 200 visits)
  • PageSpeed score below 50/100 on mobile: Google penalizes it, visitors leave
  • The site isn't mobile-friendly, while over 60% of French traffic is mobile
  • You can't edit the content yourself (total dependency on the original provider)
  • The image it projects no longer matches your positioning: a site dated to 2018 undersells a premium business
  • The site is invisible on Google and on AI (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews) for your business queries

Conversely, if the site already ranks well and converts properly, targeted optimization (speed, content, calls to action) costs 5 to 10 times less than a redesign and is often enough. A free audit settles it objectively.

Partial or full redesign: the decision table

CriteriaPartial redesignFull redesign
Typical caseDated design, sound structureTechnically obsolete site + weak SEO
Existing SEO~100% preservedTo be migrated (risky if done poorly)
Indicative budget€1,500 – 4,000€3,000 – 15,000
Timeline2 to 4 weeks4 to 10 weeks
URL changesNoOften (redirects required)
When to choose itThe substance is good, the form is datedThe site is holding the business back across the board

Simple rule: if your site already receives significant organic traffic, protecting that traffic becomes priority #1 of the project — ahead of design.

The 7-step method

Step 1 — Audit of the existing site (week 1)

Before touching anything, measure what the current site has:

  • Page inventory: full crawl, list of every existing URL
  • Pages that rank: via Google Search Console, identify pages generating impressions and clicks
  • Backlinks: which pages receive external links (they must never return a 404 after the redesign)
  • Current performance: Core Web Vitals, conversion rate, traffic sources

What isn't measured before the redesign can't be compared afterward. This audit is what lets you say, 3 months later, "the redesign worked" — with numbers.

Step 2 — Strategy and site architecture (week 1-2)

The new structure is designed from data, not taste:

  • Pages that perform keep their URL unchanged whenever possible
  • Dead pages (0 traffic, 0 backlinks, dated content) are removed with a redirect
  • Missing pages (high-potential queries with no dedicated page) are added to the plan

This is also when you define each page's conversion goal: quote request, call, form. A page with no goal is a decorative page.

Step 3 — Mockup and design (week 2-4)

Design is validated on a mockup before a single line of code. Non-negotiable points in 2026:

  • Mobile-first: the mobile mockup is validated before the desktop version
  • A clear message above the fold: who you are, for whom, what action
  • Controlled visual weight: every animation or video costs you loading speed

Step 4 — Development (week 3-6)

Development builds in SEO from the start, not as a final fix: unique title tags and meta descriptions per page, clean Hn structure, Schema.org structured data, optimized images (WebP/AVIF), target load time under 2 seconds.

Step 5 — 301 redirect plan (before launch)

This is the step that makes or breaks SEO. Every old URL must resolve: either it still exists, or it 301-redirects to the closest equivalent page.

Rules to follow:

  • Redirect page to equivalent page, never everything to the homepage (Google treats that as soft 404s)
  • Also handle variants: with/without trailing slash, http/https, www/non-www
  • Absolutely prioritize pages with backlinks and traffic
  • Keep the mapping file: it will serve as a reference for 12 months

Step 6 — QA and launch

Minimum cutover checklist:

  1. Verify the staging site is set to noindex and that the live site is not (forgetting to remove noindex in production is the single most destructive mistake there is)
  2. Test every redirect in the mapping
  3. Submit the new sitemap.xml in Google Search Console
  4. Check tracking (GA4, conversions) within the first hour
  5. Crawl the live site to detect 404s

Step 7 — Post-launch monitoring (weeks 1 to 12)

A redesign is judged over 3 months, not 3 days. Monitor weekly in Search Console: 404 errors, indexing coverage, rankings of strategic pages. A temporary 10-15% drop in the first 2 weeks is normal (Google recrawling); a 40% drop that persists signals a redirect problem.

How much does a website redesign cost?

ProviderShowcase redesign budgetWhat's includedMain risk
DIY (Wix, WordPress...)€0 – 500Your time (50-150h)SEO migration ignored, traffic lost
Freelancer€1,500 – 5,000Design + dev, variable SEOHighly inconsistent quality
Low-cost / subscription agency€50 – 150/monthAdapted templateSite not owned, minimal SEO
Custom agency€3,000 – 15,000Strategy + design + dev + full SEO migrationHigher upfront investment

The invisible but decisive line item: SEO migration (audit, mapping, redirects, monitoring). It represents 15 to 25% of the budget with a serious provider. A redesign quote that mentions neither redirects nor Search Console is a red flag.

To estimate your project precisely, our online configurator gives you a range in 2 minutes, and our guide on how much a website costs breaks down pricing by project type.

The 5 costliest redesign mistakes

  1. Redirecting all old URLs to the homepage. Google treats them as deleted pages: the SEO equity is lost.
  2. Leaving the noindex tag in production. The site disappears from Google within days. Check it on launch day, then again 7 days later.
  3. Deleting content that ranks because it "looks old." An ugly article generating 300 visits/month should be rewritten, not deleted.
  4. Changing URLs for no reason. Every URL change is a risk; only change what needs to change.
  5. Judging the result by looks. A prettier site that converts less is a failed redesign. Success metrics are defined before the project starts: traffic, leads, conversion rate.

Redesign and AI visibility: the new 2026 criterion

A 2026 redesign must prepare the site for answer engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews), which account for a growing share of business discovery:

  • Complete Schema.org structured data (Organization, LocalBusiness, FAQ, Article)
  • Factual, citable content: numbers, clear definitions, direct answers at the start of sections
  • Accessibility to AI crawlers: allow GPTBot, PerplexityBot and ClaudeBot in robots.txt if you want to be cited

We detail this approach in our guide AEO vs SEO vs GEO and our article on how to appear in ChatGPT and Perplexity.

FAQ — Website redesign

How long does a website redesign take?

Between 4 and 10 weeks for a showcase site depending on scope: roughly 1 week of audit and strategy, 2 to 3 weeks of design, 2 to 4 weeks of development, then migration and QA. Shorter timelines advertised (48h, 1 week) usually mean a template with no SEO migration work.

Does a redesign hurt Google rankings?

No, if the migration is done properly: keeping high-performing URLs, page-to-page 301 redirects, sitemap submitted to Google, and Search Console monitoring for 3 months. The risk of loss (30 to 70% of traffic) only exists when redirects are missing or mass-redirected to the homepage.

How much does a showcase site redesign cost in 2026?

Between €1,500 and 5,000 with a freelancer, and between €3,000 and 15,000 with a custom agency, SEO migration included. Budget depends on page count, content work, and technical complexity. A partial redesign (design only, structure kept) costs 40 to 60% less than a full redesign.

Should you redesign or optimize your existing site?

If the site ranks and converts but looks dated, targeted optimization is often enough (5 to 10 times cheaper). A redesign is warranted when the technical foundation is obsolete: non-responsive site, unrecoverable speed, abandoned CMS, inability to edit content. An objective audit of the existing site helps you decide before committing a budget.

Can you keep your domain name during a redesign?

Yes, and it's strongly recommended: the domain name carries the accumulated history and SEO authority. You only change domains for a strong strategic reason (rebranding), and in that case the migration requires domain-to-domain 301 redirects and an address change declaration in Google Search Console.

Conclusion: a redesign is managed with numbers

A successful website redesign rests on three pillars: a data-backed audit of the existing site, a rigorous SEO migration (page-to-page 301 redirects, Search Console monitoring), and measurable conversion goals defined before the first pixel.

At MSD Media, every redesign includes the audit, the full redirect plan, and 3 months of post-launch monitoring — because a prettier site that loses its traffic is a failure, no matter how good it looks.

Considering a redesign? Book a free 30-minute strategy audit: we'll analyze your existing site and tell you honestly whether a redesign is warranted — or not.
en.art_schemaorgfr_title: Schema.org and Structured Data: Why AI Reads Them Better Than Google
en.art_schemaorgfr_body:
Schema.org has existed since 2011. Google, Bing and Yahoo created it together. For 10 years, structured data mainly served to enrich search results (rich snippets). In 2026, its role has fundamentally changed: it has become one of the most important signals for being cited by AI engines.

What structured data is

Structured data is semantic annotation added to your page's HTML to explain to machines what your content contains. You can indicate: "this text is an organization's name," "this number is a rating," "this list is an FAQ."

The recommended format is JSON-LD (JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data), injected in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag in the page's <head>.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Organization",
  "name": "MSD Media",
  "url": "https://msd-media.com",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "addressLocality": "Annecy",
    "addressCountry": "FR"
  }
}

Why AI reads schemas better than Google does

Google uses them for rich snippets (optional)

Google uses structured data to display stars, FAQs, prices in results. But it's optional — Google can understand your content without schema, through its semantic understanding engine.

LLMs use them to build their knowledge graph

Language models (GPT-4, Gemini, Claude) process the web differently. They don't "understand" text the same way Google does. They rely on structured, consistent data to build a reliable representation of your entity.

A well-filled-out Organization schema tells them explicitly:

  • Who you are
  • Where you are
  • What you do
  • Who you are on other platforms (via sameAs)

It's pure, unambiguous signal.

Priority schemas for GEO

Organization — the most important

{
  "@type": "Organization",
  "name": "Your Agency",
  "url": "https://yoursite.com",
  "logo": {"@type": "ImageObject", "url": "https://yoursite.com/logo.webp"},
  "founder": {"@type": "Person", "name": "Your Name"},
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "addressLocality": "City",
    "postalCode": "XXXXX",
    "addressCountry": "FR"
  },
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.linkedin.com/company/...",
    "https://fr.trustpilot.com/review/...",
    "https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/..."
  ],
  "aggregateRating": {
    "@type": "AggregateRating",
    "ratingValue": "5",
    "reviewCount": "47"
  }
}

The sameAs field is especially important for GEO: it links your entity to its representations on other platforms that AI models know well.

FAQPage — for direct answers

{
  "@type": "FAQPage",
  "mainEntity": [
    {
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "How much does a landing page cost?",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "text": "A custom landing page costs between quote-based and quote-based..."
      }
    }
  ]
}

FAQs are the excerpts AI models cite verbatim most often. A well-structured FAQ with schema is 3 to 5 times more likely to be cited than an ordinary paragraph of text.

LocalBusiness — for local GEO

{
  "@type": "LocalBusiness",
  "name": "Your Business",
  "telephone": "+33XXXXXXXXX",
  "email": "contact@yoursite.com",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "123 Example Street",
    "addressLocality": "City",
    "postalCode": "XXXXX"
  },
  "areaServed": {"@type": "City", "name": "City"},
  "priceRange": "Quote-based"
}

Person — for the expert / founder

Associating a human expert with your content increases its credibility in the eyes of AI models.

{
  "@type": "Person",
  "name": "Maxens Soldan",
  "jobTitle": "Founder & CEO",
  "worksFor": {"@type": "Organization", "name": "MSD Media"},
  "sameAs": ["https://www.linkedin.com/in/maxens-soldan/"]
}

Common mistakes to avoid

MistakeImpactFix
Incomplete schema (missing required fields)Ignored by Google and AIValidate with Rich Results Test
Data inconsistent with visible contentPossible Google penaltySync schema with HTML content
sameAs pointing to incomplete profilesWeak GEO signalFill out linked profiles
Invalid JSON-LD (commas, quotes)Schema ignoredValidate with schema.org/validator
Organization without aggregateRatingLess credibilityAdd Trustpilot reviews

How to test your structured data

  1. Rich Results Test (search.google.com/test/rich-results) — official Google test
  2. Schema Markup Validator (validator.schema.org) — full schema.org validation
  3. ChatGPT / Perplexity — ask direct questions about your business and see if it's correctly identified

FAQ

Partial or full redesign: which should you budget for?

A partial redesign (€1,500 – 4,000) works when the foundation is sound: logical structure, content that ranks, correct technical setup. You modernize the design, improve calls to action, optimize speed — without touching URLs or architecture. Existing SEO is preserved ~100%, timeline is 2 to 4 weeks.

The simple test to decide: if your site gets organic traffic and generates inquiries, but looks dated → partial. If it generates nothing or runs on dead technology → full.   2. SEO migration. URL inventory, 301 redirect mapping, preserving pages with backlinks, 3 months of Search Console monitoring: 15 to 25% of the budget with a serious provider. If the quote doesn't mention it, the price is artificially low.

FAQ — Website redesign pricing

What's the average price of a website redesign in 2026?

For an SMB showcase site, budget €1,500 to 4,000 for a partial redesign (design and optimizations, structure kept) and €3,000 to 15,000 for a full agency redesign, SEO migration included. The gaps come from page count, content work, and the depth of SEO migration.

Why does a redesign sometimes cost more than building from scratch?

Because a redesign adds a project that fresh creation doesn't have: migrating the existing site. URL inventory, page-to-page 301 redirects, preserving ranking content, data carryover — this work represents 15 to 25% of the budget and determines whether your organic traffic survives. Building from scratch has nothing to protect; redesigning does.

Is a €500 redesign possible?

Yes, but it's limited to a template skin change, with no SEO migration or content work. If your current site has no traffic or rankings to protect, that's workable. If it gets organic traffic, a low-cost redesign with no redirect plan can cost you far more than it saves: 30 to 70% of traffic lost for months.

Is SEO migration really necessary?

Yes, as soon as your site gets organic traffic. Every old URL must either still exist identically or 301-redirect to its equivalent; pages with backlinks must be preserved first; the new sitemap must be submitted to Google. Without this, Google treats your pages as deleted and your accumulated rankings disappear — an asset destroyed in a single launch.

How much time should you plan for a redesign?

2 to 4 weeks for a partial redesign, 4 to 10 weeks for a full one: audit and strategy (1 week), design (2-3 weeks), development (2-4 weeks), migration and QA (1 week), then 3 months of Search Console monitoring. What it is

A web agency is a specialized team that handles the entire project: strategy, design, development, copywriting, SEO, delivery.

Agencies range from micro-agencies (2-3 people) to mid-sized agencies (10-50 people).

Pros

  • Multidisciplinary expertise: design, dev, SEO, copywriting in a single team
  • Proven process: predictable timelines and deliverables
  • Built-in conversion strategy: the goal isn't "a pretty site" but "a site that converts"
  • Accountability: an agency stakes its reputation on the work
  • Post-launch support: fixes, updates, evolutions

Cons

  • Higher price than no-code or a junior freelancer
  • Less flexibility on tech stack (each agency has its own tools)
  • Communication sometimes more formal

Can you combine all three options? Yes. For example: build a first no-code site to test, then bring in an agency for the redesign once you've validated your offer and market.

Which option for a local restaurant? For a restaurant, a no-code tool (Squarespace or Wix) can be enough if you don't have strong SEO ambitions. If you want to rank on "restaurant [city]," a local agency specialized in SEO will be more effective.
